 Cybertruck Wind-Down: 11,000-lb Tow, 63,619 Recalled [2026]
 Daniel Roth 
 Updated Nov 6, 2026 · 14 min read 
 Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027, and the news landed on November 06, 2026 with a WIRED obituary titled “RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd.” Elon Musk said on X that the line would make room for Cybercab production. That is the confirmed core. Everything else, including the harsh adjectives in the WIRED headline, is characterization.

 This piece looks at the hardware side of the story: what the truck actually specs out at, what the 63,619-vehicle recall covers, what the stainless-steel body means for the factory floor, and who gets what when a pickup line closes. We already tracked the Cox Automotive sales estimates behind the wind-down , so here we focus on the machine itself and the choices Tesla now faces.
 A note on method. Tesla does not break out Cybertruck sales in its financial reports, so any volume number you read is an outside estimate. Where we use one, we label it. Where a claim cannot be checked, we say so instead of rounding it into a fact.

 Add now What Happened: Tesla Sets Mid-2027 for the Cybertruck Wind-Down
 Reports citing Musk’s post on X say Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production around mid-2027. The stated reason is capacity. Tesla wants the floor space and the manufacturing attention at Giga Texas for Cybercab, its purpose-built autonomous vehicle. Musk did not announce an immediate stop, and nothing in the reporting says Tesla has canceled the truck or pulled it from sale today.
 That distinction matters for readers searching for answers. “Wind down” describes a planned taper with an approximate date. It does not say the last truck rolls off the line on a specific day, and it does not say owners lose support. Our earlier coverage of the mid-2027 wind-down announcement covered the first hours of the story. Since then the picture has filled in around the recall record, the sales estimates and the factory plan.

 WIRED framed the news as an obituary. Outlets such as NBC News, CBS News and Engadget ran shorter, more neutral versions that stuck to the production timeline and the Cybercab rationale. The gap between those tones tells you something. The facts are modest and the emotions are large, because the Cybertruck was always a product people had opinions about.
 What the Fact Sheet Confirms and What It Does Not
 Before the analysis, here is the line between what is established and what is not. We sorted every claim we plan to use into one of two bins. The first bin holds items tied to Tesla’s own configurator, Tesla’s owner manual, a reported NHTSA recall, or Musk’s reported post on X. The second bin holds numbers and labels that come from estimates or opinion.
 Claim Status Basis 
 Production winds down around mid-2027 Confirmed as reported Musk’s post on X, per news reports 
 Reason is more Cybercab production Confirmed as reported Same post 
 Recall covers 63,619 trucks built Nov. 13, 2023 to Oct. 11, 2025 Confirmed as reported NHTSA recall, per reporting 
 325-mile EPA-estimated range, 11,000 lb towing, 4.1 s 0-60 Confirmed Tesla configurator 
 11,586 U.S. sales in first nine months of 2026 Unconfirmed Cox Automotive estimate, not a Tesla release 
 Truck “initially” cost $39,999 Unconfirmed No official Tesla price record found 
 Cybertruck is “dead” or canceled Unconfirmed No official statement says so 
 “Unloved, Unwanted, Utterly Absurd” Opinion WIRED headline, not a measurable finding 
 We will keep to that split for the rest of the article. If a number appears later without a Tesla, NHTSA or Cox label, it is arithmetic on one of the numbers above.
 Cybertruck Specs and Prices on Tesla’s Configurator
 Judged purely as hardware, the Cybertruck’s published numbers are not weak. Tesla’s configurator lists a 325-mile EPA-estimated range, 11,000 pounds of towing capacity and a 4.1-second 0-60 mph time for the configuration it shows. Tesla’s owner manual puts overall length at 223.74 inches (5,682.9 mm) and payload ratings between 2,000 and 2,500 pounds depending on configuration.
 Spec Figure Source 
 EPA-estimated range 325 miles Tesla configurator 
 Towing capacity 11,000 lb Tesla configurator 
 0-60 mph 4.1 seconds Tesla configurator 
 Premium All-Wheel Drive price $74,990 Tesla configurator 
 Higher configuration price $84,990 Tesla configurator 
 Overall length 223.74 in (5,682.9 mm) Tesla owner manual 
 Payload rating 2,000 to 2,500 lb Tesla owner manual 
 Two things stand out. First, the gap between the $74,990 Premium All-Wheel Drive truck and the $84,990 configuration is $10,000. Second, the headline performance numbers (a 4.1-second sprint with an 11,000-pound tow rating) describe a truck that works on paper. The case against the Cybertruck was never a spec-sheet case. It was a case about price, fit, finish and trust.
 The 63,619-Truck Recall in Context
 The recall figure that anchors this story covers 63,619 Cybertrucks built for the U.S. between November 13, 2023 and October 11, 2025, according to reporting on the NHTSA filing. The window is long. It spans most of the truck’s production life to date, which suggests the issue touched nearly the whole fleet rather than one bad batch.
 We should be careful about what a recall number proves. A recall count measures how many vehicles are covered by a safety remedy, not how many failed. It also does not equal sales. Still, when a recall window of roughly two years lines up with a production run, the covered count becomes a useful ceiling check on volume. It tells you the U.S. build count in that window was at least 63,619, which is a number the company and regulators both stand behind.
 That ceiling check is worth holding against the Cox estimates in the next section. Cox figures are outside estimates and the recall figure comes from a federal filing. When you want one hard anchor for how many Cybertrucks exist on U.S. roads, the recall count is the sturdier one.
 Sales Estimates: What the Cox Automotive Numbers Can and Cannot Say
 Reporting attributes an estimate of 11,586 U.S. Cybertruck sales in the first nine months of 2026 to Cox Automotive. We list it as unconfirmed because Tesla never published it. Cox builds such figures from registration and transaction data, and they carry error bars that Tesla’s own numbers would not.
 Even so, estimates from a firm like Cox are the best public read on a vehicle Tesla does not report separately. The trend that coverage describes, a steep fall from the launch rush, matches what our own earlier piece on the 48% sales drop laid out. The takeaway: demand cooled hard, and the wind-down date arrives after that cooling, not before it.
 One more caution. A viral claim says the Cybertruck “initially” cost $39,999. We found no official Tesla price record supporting that figure, so we do not treat it as fact. The prices we can stand behind are the configurator’s $74,990 and $84,990 entries. Anyone comparing launch promises to today’s sticker should hunt for a primary source first.
 Why Giga Texas and Its Stainless-Steel Body Equipment Matter
 Cybertruck manufacturing happens at Gigafactory Texas, according to reporting that points to the facility’s specialized stainless-steel-body equipment. That detail is the hardware heart of the story. Most pickups are stamped from steel or aluminum sheet with decades of supplier tooling behind them. The Cybertruck’s exterior skeleton uses a different material and a different set of machines.
 What a Material-First Truck Does to a Factory
 Specialized forming and joining gear is expensive to install and awkward to repurpose. When a line is built around one body material, the equipment may not carry over to a different vehicle without rework. We cannot say from the sources how much of that gear Tesla will strip out, move or leave idle. What we can say is that a company does not usually reassign floor space like this without a clear internal view of the cost.
 The Open Question on Tooling
 The reports say Cybercab gets the room. They do not say what happens to the stainless-steel equipment afterward. That gap is where the interesting hardware questions sit. Does the gear get sold, stored or scrapped? Does Tesla keep a small service line running for parts? None of that is confirmed, and anyone claiming certainty is guessing.
 Cybercab Takes the Floor Space
 The stated reason for the wind-down is more Cybercab output, and Tesla’s engineering leadership has been talking about that line in public. In remarks relayed by EV Wire, vehicle engineering vice president Lars Moravy said the listed capacity of the Cybercab line reflects the rate Tesla runs today, while the line’s actual capacity is considerably higher. He also said Tesla builds at the rate its Robotaxi service needs vehicles.
 Read together, those points describe a production plan tied to service demand rather than to retail pickup sales. That is a different business than selling a truck through a showroom or website. It also fits Tesla’s wider pivot toward machines that earn revenue from software and services, a theme we saw in the Optimus production timeline , where the company again set a long-range hardware goal with a year of work still ahead.
 From a pure factory-economics angle, the swap makes sense on paper. A line that makes a low-volume, high-complexity pickup is a poor use of scarce floor space when a robotaxi line can run closer to continuous demand. Whether the Cybercab ramp delivers on that logic is a separate question, and one Tesla has yet to prove at scale.
 What Musk and Moravy Actually Said
 Direct quotes in this story are scarce, so we limit ourselves to those we could verify. Musk’s post, as relayed in the verified quote set, read: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” per his X account .

 When a commenter called the news the end of an era, Musk replied, “True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time,” according to The Drive . That reply is the closest thing to an official statement on owners. It signals continued presence on the road, though it does not promise parts, service levels or software support terms.
 On the Cybercab side, Tesla’s Lars Moravy said, “We’ve definitely been bursting the Cybercab line to see how fast we can run it,” as quoted by EV Wire . He also said, “Right now, we’re building at the rate that the Robotaxi service needs the vehicles.” Those two lines frame the Cybercab line as tested for speed but throttled by demand.
 Note the gap. None of these statements gives a Cybertruck unit count, a last-build date or a service commitment. They give a direction. Treat anything more specific as unverified until Tesla files it.
 Competitive Comparison: The Electric Pickup Field
 Current coverage places the Cybertruck against the Ford F-150 Lightning, Rivian R1T, Chevrolet Silverado EV and GMC Sierra EV. We have not gathered a fresh, sourced spec set for each rival, so we do not publish side-by-side numbers here. Mixing a verified Tesla spec sheet with unverified rival figures would produce a table that looks authoritative and is not.
 What we can do is compare strategy. Tesla chose a distinct body material and a distinct shape. That choice gave the Cybertruck an unmistakable look and also tied the program to a narrow set of manufacturing methods. The other four trucks on that list do not carry that particular manufacturing bet, according to the coverage we reviewed, which leaves Tesla as the outlier.
 The wind-down, if it goes as reported, leaves Tesla without a pickup in a segment where its legacy-automaker rivals plan to keep competing. That is a real strategic cost, even if Tesla views the trade as worthwhile. A company giving up a truck slot hands the work-truck buyer to someone else, and truck buyers tend to be loyal once they pick a brand.
 Historical Context: A Truck Built Around a Material
 The Cybertruck reached the road well after Tesla first showed it, and the gap between showroom promise and delivered product has shaped its story ever since. The recall window in the NHTSA filing starts on November 13, 2023, which gives a clear marker for when regulated production was under way.
 Since then the truck has served as a test of how far a carmaker can push a manufacturing idea. Stainless-steel exteriors make a strong brand statement. They also leave less room for the incremental fixes that conventional trucks accept through years of model-year updates. A recall that spans two years of builds shows the cost of that tight design box.
 Tesla has faced tough hardware stories before. Our report on the Powerwall 3 failing at one year and requiring an RMA showed a similar pattern, where a fresh product ran into reliability questions after real-world use. Both cases underline the same lesson about launching complex hardware quickly.
 Market Impact: What the Wind-Down Signals for Tesla
 For investors, the Cybertruck was never the main earnings driver. Its role was halo and technology demonstration. Closing the line therefore changes Tesla’s story more than its near-term numbers. The company is telling the market that autonomous vehicles now outrank a flagship consumer truck for factory priority.

 That message arrives during a rough week for Tesla and its sister companies. We reported how Tesla and SpaceX lost $456B in two days after the midterms , and the political climate has sharpened scrutiny of hardware programs. A separate look at the three risks Democrats pose to SpaceX and Tesla hardware covers the regulatory side. Neither piece links the Cybertruck decision to politics, and we do not either.
 The practical read is straightforward. Tesla is cutting a low-volume product to put more weight behind a vehicle it believes can earn recurring revenue. Whether that bet pays off depends on Cybercab regulation, safety performance and public acceptance, none of which the Cybertruck decision settles.
 What Owners and Fleet Buyers Keep
 Owners want to know what the news means for the truck in their driveway. Musk’s reply that the fleet will be around for a long time points to continued road presence. Our guide to what owners keep when the line ends goes through the details. The table below summarizes what we know and what remains open.
 Group What is known What is open 
 Current owners Musk says the fleet will stay on the road for a long time Parts supply, service terms and software support length 
 Recalled trucks (63,619) Remedy covers builds from Nov. 13, 2023 to Oct. 11, 2025 Completion rates and the repair timeline 
 Prospective buyers Configurator lists $74,990 and $84,990 trucks today Last order date and final build date 
 Fleet and commercial users Payload rating of 2,000 to 2,500 lb and 11,000 lb towing Whether Tesla offers a replacement pickup 
 Giga Texas workers Cybercab gets the capacity Staffing moves, tooling disposition 
 If you hold a Cybertruck, the sensible step is to confirm your recall status through Tesla and NHTSA and keep service records. If you are considering buying one before the window closes, treat the date as approximate. “Around mid-2027” is a target, not a contract.
 Five Predictions for the Cybertruck Through 2027
 These are our forecasts, not reported facts. We built them from the confirmed items above and from how carmakers usually handle a model’s last year.
 Final-year demand blip. Announced endings often pull forward buyers who wanted a collectible. We expect some bump in orders once the end date firms up, though Cox-style estimates will be the only way to see it.
 More detail from Tesla on service. Owner pressure will push Tesla to put parts and support commitments in writing before mid-2027.
 The date will slip or shrink. “Around mid-2027” leaves room. Manufacturing wind-downs rarely hit a single day, and we expect a tapering run rather than a hard stop.
 No direct pickup successor soon. Tesla’s stated focus is Cybercab. We do not expect a new Tesla pickup announcement in the near term.
 A used-market story. Once new production ends, resale values and certified pre-owned policies will become the next headline. Watch pricing data from used-car trackers.
 Any of these could miss. The reporting gives us a direction and a rough date, and everything past that is judgment.
 Reading the “Unloved, Unwanted and Utterly Absurd” Label
 WIRED’s headline is a strong piece of opinion writing, and it deserves to be read as such. “Unloved” and “unwanted” sound like measurable claims. They are not. A production line does not close because a headline says so. “Absurd” is pure taste.
 The measurable parts are narrower. Cox Automotive’s estimates, which are outside numbers, point to a steep sales fall. The recall covers 63,619 trucks. Tesla has chosen to give the Cybertruck’s floor space to another vehicle. Those facts support a story of a product that did not meet its early promise. They do not prove that nobody wanted the truck.
 The takeaway: judge the wind-down by the filings and the factory plan, not by the adjectives. A hardware program can be flawed and costly and still have buyers who like it. We cannot measure that either way from the sources.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is the Cybertruck officially canceled?
 No. Reports say Musk announced on X that production will wind down around mid-2027 to make room for Cybercab. No source we reviewed says Tesla canceled the truck or stopped sales today. Claims that it is “dead” are not confirmed.
 When exactly does Cybertruck production end?
 The only timing on record is “around mid-2027.” Tesla has not published a last-build date. Treat the window as approximate.
 How many Cybertrucks were recalled?
 A reported NHTSA recall covered 63,619 Cybertrucks built for the U.S. between November 13, 2023 and October 11, 2025. A recall count shows how many trucks the remedy covers, not how many failed.
 What does the Cybertruck cost?
 Tesla’s configurator lists Premium All-Wheel Drive at $74,990 and another configuration at $84,990. A claim that it initially cost $39,999 has no official Tesla price record behind it, so we treat it as unconfirmed.
 What are the main Cybertruck specs?
 Tesla’s configurator lists a 325-mile EPA-estimated range, 11,000 pounds of towing capacity and a 4.1-second 0-60 mph time for the configuration it shows. The owner manual lists length at 223.74 inches and payload ratings of 2,000 to 2,500 pounds.
 How many Cybertrucks has Tesla sold in 2026?
 Tesla does not report Cybertruck sales separately. Cox Automotive estimates, as cited in reports, put U.S. sales at 11,586 for the first nine months of 2026. That figure is an outside estimate and remains unconfirmed.
 Where is the Cybertruck built?
 At Gigafactory Texas, according to reporting that points to the plant’s specialized stainless-steel-body equipment.
 Will current owners keep getting support?
 Musk replied on X that the fleet will be around for a long time. Tesla has not published parts or software support terms tied to the wind-down, so owners should watch for official guidance.
